(1) the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) plays a major role in the regulation of autonomic thermoregulatory responses in rats and humans, and that (2) this role is mediated via the hypothalamus, and that (3) ACC neurons that are activated by changes in core body temperature are located in the prelimbic area and project to the hypothalamus.

(1) the preoptic area of the hypothalamus is the primary site in the brain for the control of behavioral thermoregulatory responses and that (2) it is also a site for the control of autonomic thermoregulatory effector responses.
the prefrontal cortex plays an important role in behavioral thermoregulatory responses, and that the prefrontalcortex and the hypothalamo-preoptic area are interconnected.

the role of the hypothalamus in thermoregulation and with the neuronal mechanisms of the hypothalamic control of autonomic effector systems.
the neural basis of behavioral thermoregulatory responses, and our approach to the problem is to study the effects of brain lesions on thermoregulatory behavior.

the thermoregulation in mammals depends upon the interaction of many brain areas and the hypothalamo-preoptic region is the major site of thermoregulatory integration.
the prefrontal cortex is not essential for the control of behavioral thermoregulatory responses in the rat.
the preoptic area, the anterior hypothalamus, and the ventromedial hypothalamus are the most important thermosensitive regions in the rat.

the hypothalamus, the brainstem and spinal cord, and the neocortex are all involved in thermoregulatory control, but the hypothalamus is the most important.
